speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are proceeded with I desire to draw the attention of the Government to an article which appears in the press of Canada this morning, evidently despatched by the Canadian Press from London, England. It refers to an article in a British paper of the standing of which I have no knowledge, but inasmuch as the article has doubtless, through the Canadian Press, received very wide circulation-possibly world-wide circulation -and as, in my judgment it is defamatory to the honour of Canada I wish to call it to the attention of the Government and ask what action they propose to take in the matter. The article in question refers to the late arbitration on the value of the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and I shall quote a short sentence which reads as follows:	.

It is not more than two years since the manipulators of Ottawa, by daring and unscrupulous trickery, befooled this railway organization into an arbitration.
Later it refers to one of the arbitrators, Hon. Mr. Taft, as "a man not likely to be amenable to Canadian political and financial pressure," thereby implying that the Board of Arbitrators was subjected to political and financial pressure in the discharge of an onerous duty. Further on the article says:
If some Central American country swindled British investors out of not less than $48,000,000 by methods which were used in Canada, we think collision with the Monroe Doctrine might be risked in an effort to do something about it.
Whatever may be thought of the merits or demerits of the policy of acquisition I am sure that all the members of the House- of this House and the last-are agreed that nothing but honourable methods on the part of Canada were adopted as between this country and the British shareholders

nothing but the most honourable and fair methods throughout. A newspaper article defaming individuals may perhaps be lightly treated, but such an article defaming a nation, and circulating throughout the world, is not a matter we can afford wholly to ignore. A Government exercises some supervision over such matters in so far as they may impugn the honour of another country. The British Government has its obligations in this regard, the same as the Government of any country. I have not had the opportunity of mentioning the matter to the Prime Minister, nor to the Government, but I call their attention to it now and ask that they advise us now if possible, if not, later, what they propose to do with regard to this article that has gained such worldwide circulation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In accordance with an intimation previously given, I desire to move now this resolution on which will be based an Interim Supply Bill covering one-quarter of the present Estimates:
Resolved, that a sum not exceeding $76,499,371.88, being one-fourth of the amount of each of the several items to be voted as set forth in the main estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1923, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of Parliament, be granted to His Majesty, on account, for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1923.
I am asking for one-quarter, which will cover Supply for three months. In some cases only one-sixth has been taken; and if my hon. friends opposite prefer that the Interim Supply be limited to one-sixth, I shall have no objection; but we shall be making, as it were, two bites of a cherry. The time is not far distant when we shall have to have a second motion, and if it be agreeable, I shall take one-fourth. At a previous sitting, there was some discussion as to the procedure as regards this matter; but I think there will be a rather general recognition of the propriety of the motion, so I assume that it will go through without opposition.

I am afraid I am very much where I was the other day. The only difficulty in connection with this matter is my hon. friend himself, his hon. leader, (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his party. We had an idea that the King's business had to be carried on in a particular

way, and one of the ways which, as we then thought, were necessary, was this very question of interim supply. When the matter was under discussion the other day, I told my hon. friend that he could possibly remove a good many objections which we might have to this matter, if he would indicate wherein he was wrong last year and whether or not the practice which, as we pointed out last year, had obtained from time-well it is not immemorial, because we have not had a Parliament for that length of time, but practically from time immemorial, so far as Parliament is concerned-was wrong and whether the practice insisted on last year was right; whether it is wrong, immoral and improper to do this sort of thing or whether, for the purpose of obtaining campaign literature, it was thought to be a good thing to force a government, that required this interim supply to carry on the public service, to employ the closure. If the latter be the reason, we are not following my hon. friend in any of those tactics. If it be right that the public business should go on-and we used to think that it was- and the real motive of last year was something along the line which I have described, there will be no difficulty this year, because what the Opposition wants to do is to see the public business carried on. I desire, however, to point out to my hon. friend that last Friday he stated that his position then and his position now were not at all contradictory. If my hon. friend's position is: Last year, because the House had had ample opportunity to consider the Estimates, and did consider them, and knew something about them, it was a wrong thing to pass interim supply; and this year, because the Estimates have not yet been reached and we have not yet considered them, this proposal of interim supply is proper-if that be the position, my hon. friend is not inconsistent. But I desire to point out to the House that last year on the 8th of March the Estimates were tabled, and on the 15th of March we started going into committee on the Estimates. We were in committee on the Estimates practically all the time from then on until the 7th of April when this question of interim supply was brought up, with the result that we could receive no accommodation. On the 13th of April the item was passed after a good deal of discussion and after several rather heated arguments as to the way in which supply was being blocked by the then Opposition. Last year, the interim supply vote was put through

Interim Supply
only on the 13th of April, so that every opportunity was given to the House to go into the Estimates, and every member knew exactly what the Estimates were and what they meant. No attempt was made to rush the House. On the other hand, the then Opposition refused to accommodate the government in the conduct of public business after having had full six weeks' time for consideration of the Estimates and of the demands which the government were putting forward.
I have pointed out that there is a great deal of difference between the attitude then taken by my hon. friend and the attitude which is being taken to-day. My hon. friend's attitude of last year is really the chief point of difficulty which we have on this side of the House as regards giving consent. It may be that my hon. friend believes he is consistent because he thinks, with a ministry which is blessed and honoured by his presence, he has the absolute right of interim supply without delay, whereas, on the other hand, any other ministry is to be denied it. If consistency be advanced on that ground, I entirely agree with my hon. friend, but I hardly think he is going to advance that. I invited an explanation before our consent was further asked, but my hon. friend has given no explanation. He says that the business of the country requires this vote. Last year he held the view that the business of the country was requiring too many votes; that there was too much business. If volume of business to be done with the burdens that were then upon the country, many cf which burdens have since disappeared, and if urgency and pressure constituted the real reasons, there would have been no trouble with my hon. friend giving consent to interim supply last year. We realize that business has to be carried on, but our difficulty is to square what my hon. friend is doing this year with what was declared to be a settled policy of his party last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If what my hon. friend says is correct, I do not think there should be the slightest difficulty in our coming to an arrangement. The position taken by the Opposition last year was that the Government should not try to force the Estimates through the House of Commons by closure, and that there should be no attempt to pass a one-sixth vote without any opportunity of conference between the two sides of the House. The whole point was that a conference between the Government and the Opposition should
be held before the House was asked to vote an interim supply;the Opposition were quite willing after a conference to give the Government whatever was needed to carry on the business of the country. I have by me the remarks I made in the House last year, and I may quote from them for the benefit of my hon. friend. Speaking on April 12 in reference to a statement made on April 7 I said:
I pointed out at that time that we of the Opposition had no desire to embarrass the Government in the matter of any amount which might be necessary to pay salaries and wages, and, indeed, to carry on the public service to the extent that might be absolutely necessary.
I pointed out that it was customary, when interim supply was desired, for a conference to be held between both sides of the House, and I left the door open very wide to hon. gentlemen opposite to meet the Opposition in a friendly and courteous way in that connection.
Elsewhere in the course of my remarks on April 7 I said:
But in taking this stand we have no desire in any way to embarrass or penalize the Civil Service because of any neglect on the part of the Government. We will be perfectly willing to consider any arrangement with a view of providing what may be necessary in the way of salaries both for the inside and outside services. As respects other expenditures, however, we contend that except as agreed upon, this Parliament should have the full right of examining in the closest detail every item of the Estimates before voting any portion of them.
I said further in conclusion:
May I repeat, in a word, the position which we take? We are ready at any time to meet hon. gentlemen opposite in conference, to agree to give them what is necessary in the way of meeting salaries and wages for employees of the public service. We are prepared to go further and to give them what is needed to carry on the public service of this country in a manner which will not embarrass public business, which will help to maintain the good faith of the Government, and its credit, which will enable the Government to carry out commitments to which my hon. friend has referred; but this must be as a result of a conference between both sides of this House, surrounding whatever may be granted with such conditions as, in the public interest, seem to be absolutely necessary at the present time.
That was our position, and if my hon. friends opposite will take the same attitude on this occasion there should not be the slightest difficulty in our coming to an agreement as to what portion of the Estimates are to be permitted to pass as an Interim Supply. We are asking of our friends opposite nothing more than we when in Opposition, were prepared, to concede to the Government of the day. I may, however, point out to my hon friend this circumstance, which I think is an important
Interim Supply

consideration: The Government of the day fixed the time at which the general elections should be held. The date was fixed as December 6. As a consequence it was not humanly possible for the present Government to prepare the business of Parliament in shorter order than we have despatched it. I might also remind my hon. friends that when we were discussing the question of the Interim Supply last year, the Government of the day had not at the time brought down the Auditor General's report in full. We, on this side, laid the Auditor General's report in full on the Table of the House the very day the House opened.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend has what he wants. However, all we ask is that hon. gentlemen opposite shall not embarrass the public service; and if they prefer a conference before we press for this Interim Supply, we are ready to meet them and discuss matters, and withhold any part of the Estimates which they would like to have reserved for further consideration.

The Prime Minister, on this question, is in the fortunate position, in which he will often find himself in the House, of being able to quote himself on either side of the question, whichever happens for the time being to be the side that he wishes to advance. It is true that last session, after the motion was introduced for one-sixth of the Estimates to be voted in bulk, the Opposition took the stand that there should be a conference between themselves and the Government, and that they were ready to confer on the question as to the voting of salaries to the civil servants. That was the first proposal, after the introduction of the motion for one-sixth of the Estimates: But the session before, the leader of the Opposition peremptorily notified Parliament that in the session to come, namely, last session, the Opposition would unconditionally oppose all bulk Estimates, whether a quarter, a sixth, or any other proportion. No conditions whatever were attached; we were simply notified that that was the last of bulk Estimates that 
were to go through this Parliament except over the heads of, and by closure on, Opposition. Well, in the face of that notification, would it have been courteous for us to have gone to the then leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and ask him whether he had recanted? We did not feel that that would be complimentary to the hon. gentleman, and we did not do it. We did him the honour of taking him at his word. I have this quotation from the speech the hon. gentleman made the year before. We introduced our Estimates and submitted them to Parliament; and we were told-not the day that we brought down our Estimates, not before a single member of the House knew anything about what the Government was going to request, not before a single item of the Estimates had been considered, but a month after they had been presented to the House, and after Parliament had had an opportunity to consider them for days and weeks together -we were told that we should have a conference with the Opposition and that they would be ready to vote salaries so that the civil servants might not go without their pay. That was the second position the Opposition took. Well, it was pointed out that if salaries were voted, and there was no money to work with, there would not be much use in keeping the civil servants employed. The Opposition were pledging their willingness to allow the officers of the Pension Board and all the staff to be paid their salaries, but they were taking the position that no pensions should be paid. They were willing, for example, to support the Soldiers' Settlement Board, and pay the thousands of men and women employed therein, but they were not willing that any soldier settlers should get help. When that was pointed out the Opposition changed their attitude. They shifted their position and said: Well, we will let the salaries go through, and if you will confer with us we will let the necessary services be voted. The Government then took the stand that the Opposition had had the Estimates before them for at least five weeks. It was then, not the 27th of March but the 7th or 8th day of April, eight days after the fiscal year had closed; and we said that, having had the Estimates before them for that length of time, if they could show us any items that should be reserved, as respects which they thought the one-sixth should not apply, we would confer with them on any one of those. Now that seemed to me to be reason

Interim Supply
able last year, and it seems to me to be reasonable to-day. But what is the circumstance this year? The Government introduced the Estimates one day and now, on the next day, they demand one-sixth. They said: We will let you study the Estimates over Sunday and we will be back on Monday, when we want this portion voted. How different hon. gentlemen are to-day from what they were a year ago. No; what they wanted a year ago was merely to be able to go to the country and say that the Government had forced its hand into the Treasury and extracted millions of money, using in this House the power of the closure, so that the Opposition, representing the people, were not given a chance to discuss the votes.
They declared. "We were broken through, overcome by closure, the voice of the people was stifled and the money taken from the Treasury." That was all they were asking for a year ago, and that they got, and hon. gentlemen to my left and the people they represent listened to the tale of woe about the extortion of money by closure. The actual circumstances were simply the circumstances I have just disclosed. All manner of time was given for discussion.
Now I do say this. The last thing I want to do is to imitate the tactics of the Opposition last year. But I want to discharge as best I can the duties that now appertain to me as leader of the Opposition. I do not think we know enough about these Estimates to vote in bulk at all; I do not think it is necessary yet to vote them in bulk. We did not take the vote last year till 13th April. The payments made at the end of March can be taken out of the Estimates passed last year. The next payments will be coming due about the 15th April, and I say we ought to know more about the Estimates-we ought especially to be able to go over them carefully and see whether there are not items that should be exempted from this bulk vote-before we are asked to vote it to-day.
^Furthermore, we ought to have information not only as to what the Estimates were last year, but what amount was spent last year. The Government have sought in bringing down these Estimates-which, anyone who knows the slightest thing about public affairs would easily understand would necessarily be very much smaller than last year's Estimates-to convey the impression that the axe has been unmercifully wielded and that the people of this country, as a consequence of the economy of hon. gentlemen opposite, are going to save all sorts of
money in taxation. They compare the main Estimates this year with the whole Estimates last year, and forget to advise the public that there will be Supplementaries this year the same as last. The fact of the matter is that, notwithstanding we are a year farther away from the war, notwithstanding the fact that all war services are necessarily and rightly contracting, and have been contracting every year since the war, we are asked to vote main Estimates this year amounting to fifty million dollars more, I do not doubt, than the whole expenditure of last year.
Comparing the main Estimates this yeav with the main Estimates last year there is a difference of $113,000,000. Of that $113,000,000 difference $81,000,000 odd is made up of advances necessarily made last year on account of the Canadian National railway betterments, because we had just taken over one great system and had to vote $89,000,000 to put it in shape. The advances made last year for the railways of this country are not needed this year, for the most obvious reason in the world,-that last year the railways of this country were put into condition which was necessary in order that the people might get from the system the service they were entitled to. Instead of $50,000,000 being required this year on account of the Canadian National railway only $42,800,000 is required; the Canadian National railways are showing improvement; these railways that, according to hon. gentlemen opposite, had brought the country to the brink of ruin so that they had to come in and arrest the hand of nationalization,-yes, force back the hand of nationalization- in order to save this nation from bankruptcy and despair. The railways are showing improvement. The Grand Trunk last year, having just been taken over, required $89,687,633, not for a year, mark you, but for a year and a quarter, because the moneys voted for the railways last year covered fifteen months from January 1,1921 to March 31, 1922. They took care as well of the Grand Trunk on its being taken over at a time when there were large outstai. fling obligations that had to be provided for if the railway was to stand up at all. Necessarily that $89,000,000 is not required this year; the vote for that system therefore is only $25,750,000. The Grand Trunk Pacific, which also had been taken over just the year before, required last year $26,000,000 in assistance. This year the vote is $15,900,000. There is no individual in Canada who in honesty of mind, would attribute for a moment any intention tc
Interim Supply

economize on the part of a government in relation to advances to assist, when those advances, having been made, are necessarily not required to be made again. That accounts for $81,237,000.
Then there is the Soldier Settlement Board. I wonder if the Government are economizing with the soldier settlers. Last year the vote was $35,017,000, and this year it is $12,000,000, a difference of $23,017,000. That can hardly be attributed to economy. It is because of the fact that we took care of the soldiers when they returned, obviating the necessity of taking care of them later on and having them look after themselves in the meantime. I do not at the moment question that the vote asked for this year will be sufficient to take care of the situation. Indeed, it turns out that of the $35,017,000 voted last year, something less than $12,000,000 was required, because large sums of money came in from the soldiers themselves and took care of a large amount of what was required.
Then also, as we recede from the war the number of men to be taken care of in the Government institutions naturally diminishes, and as it diminishes the requirements of the Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment decline. Last year's vote was very many millions-I do not know the exact figure-less than the year before. This year the vote is $4,956,500 less than last year, and that can be saved, I do not doubt at all, without very much necessity of the economical pruning knife of the Minister of Finance. The vote last year, I understand, was $21,000,000 less than the vote of the preceding year, and this year the decrease is $4,956,500.
The housing appropriation, which is not spent, but merely loaned to provincial governments, naturally goes down as we recede from the war and war conditions. The decrease there is $2,449,920. It is not a matter of economy in the slightest degree. Those items account for $111,660,000 of the $113,626,000.
The shipbuilding programme brought down in 1919, and never added to since, was completed altogether, I am inclined to think, or within a few dollars. I do not know that it will be suggested that it is an exercise of very great wisdom not to build the ships over again. They are built already. The money does not need to be spent over again. That accounts for $10,000,000 odd. So, aside from those items to which the word "economy" has no application whatever, the Government

is $8,000,000 over the Estimates of last year, and is approximating $50,000,000 over the expenditure of last year all told.
That is an outline of the situation. Consequently, the argument advanced last year that, the expenditure being more than was required ten years before they could not be asked to give the same liberal consideration to a vote on a bulk estimate, has no application whatever. Indeed, it turns against hon. gentlemen opposite, for in every respect in which economy can be exercised to public advantage hon. gentlemen opposite are already $8,000,000 and more over the vote of last year.
I notice a decrease of $235,906 in the vote for the Imperial War Graves Commission. That is accounted for, of course, by the fact that the war graves have been attended to and do not require to be attended to twice over. I do not presume that hon. gentlemen would claim to exercise economy in attending to the graves of our soldiers. It is simply a matter of the work having been done and not requiring to be done again.
Again, last year a vote of $500,000 was required under the Canada Temperance Act for taking the vote in Ontario. That is not required this year. A vote of $500,000 was taken as well last year for the Battlefields Memorial. That is not necessary this year. So the Government, if we leave out those items as to which the word "economy" has no application whatever, is $10,000,009 over last year's main Estimates, with the supplementary Estimates still to come, and approximately $50,000,000 over last year's actual expenditure.
That is a summary of the position today. Consequently it behooves the Opposition, it behooves the supporters of the Government as well, to see to it that these Estimates are scrupulously proven, and before we vote any Estimates in bulk we ought to at least have a sufficient opportunity to go over the votes one by one and make up our minds whether or not there are items as respects which the bulk vote should not apply. That is all I asked of the Opposition last year; but they were not satisfied. Nothing could exceed the unreasonableness of the attitude they took-except perhaps the representations, or rather the misrepresentations they made in the course of the campaign. I do not want to follow their example; but I do ask that this vote stand for a few days, at all events, in order that we may have an opportunity to go over the Estimates

with care, and then to confer with the Government concerning such items as in our opinion should be exempt from the bulk vote we are asked to pass.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am much more interested in getting this appropriation made in the proper way than I am in reviving the discussion of last year. But I am surprised that my right hon. friend has deemed it expedient to enter at this stage into a general discussion of the Estimates. He says we have been claiming great economy. When? Where?
In the press.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not a single word. We brought down the Estimates and laid them on the table; no member of the Government said a single word about them. My right hon. friend seems to have got the notion that the people may themselves see something in the direction of economy. I hope they will, but if they do, it will have to be of their own motion; it will not be due to anything that has been said by any member of the Government. My right hon. friend has invented, as it were, a boast of economy, for we have been absolutely silent on the subject.
* The right hon. gentleman says also that we have brought down the Estimates in such a way as to make a comparison with those of last year. Have we not brought them down in the usual form? He also says that the supplementary Estimates have to come. That is true, 'but has it not been so every year? In what other form could the Estimates have been brought down, so far as comparison is concerned, than that in which they are set out in this blue book? My right hon. friend implies that we have been making exceptional claims for economy. He is drawing upon his imagination. He is alarmed by the thought that the people may on their own account see that there is economy; therefore, he feels it necesary to warn them that there is none.
Mr. Chairman, we have no desire to press these Estimates. The vital difference between the position to-day and that of last year is, as has been stated by the Prime Minister, that the Estimates last year should not have been pressed before the House as they were without a proper conference. I have under my hand correspondence which I have had with my esteemed friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). Even before the present Estimates were brought down, I wrote to him, informed him of our intention, and
said I wanted his co-orperation. I intimated that while it might be convenient to have a general vote-one-quarter of the whole, or one-sixth, as he might prefer- if hon. members wanted to reserve any portion of the Estimates we were quite ready to do so. There will be no closure in this matter, Mr. Chairman; this vote will be given freely and voluntarily or not at all. If my right hon. friend is trying to lay some plans whereby he may force us to bring on the closure, I tell him at once that his effort will fail. Closure is necessary, in a measure, I suppose, in some things, but it is not the desire of this Government to use it in a case like this. If hon. gentlemen opposite want these Estimates delayed for a few days, I am willing that it shall be so. The leader of the Opposition has said that he has had no time to examine them. Well, he has made quite a criticism of them; if he has not had time to examine them, I do not know where he got the amazing amount of information he had to-day, 'be it correct or not.
As I have said, my great desire is to have this appropriation made in a fair and proper way; it wil be done that way or not at all. My right hon. friend says he wants the matter delayed for a few days; I at once agree to that. My only desire is to provide for the urgent and pressing needs of the public service. If my hon. friends opposite, now or later, stand in the way of those needs being met, they will have to take the responsibility for doing so.

I desire to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his frankness and his fairness. He says he has made no claim for economy. That is right, and he could not fairly have done so. But many claims have been made for him -made to such an extent, indeed, that my hon. friend's own statement, strong as it is, and respected as he himself is, would seem to be unnecessary on the present occasion. He has many influences working for him, and they have been working very well indeed. The claim of economy certainly came from somewhere-a statment to the press making claims for economies amounting, if I remember rightly, to twenty-three per cent in respect of the main Estimates. However, my hon. friend now agrees that there is no claim to be made for economies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not that there is no claim to be made, but that none has been made.

fMr. Fielding.]
These items, as I have pointed out, have little if anything to do with the cost of government administration proper; they relate to projects that had previously been carried or to liabilities that had previously been met. Of course, I do not know the last state of the accounts; the Minister of Finance knows that. But I want to point out one of the reasons why we ought to consider carefully these Estimates. Down to the 20th of this month, when the last statement was issued, the total amount spent out of the consolidated fund amounted to $307,000,000. Of course it is true the financial year has not yet expired, but the late government did not run above that amount. On the other hand we have requisitions here to the amount of $466,000,000 in the main Estimates. It is true that my hon. friend opposite has a right to set up other claims, although that used not to be done. For example last year, down to 20th March, under the accounting practices of governments of the past, there was a surplus- that surplus representing the difference between Consolidated Fund receipts and Consolidated Fund payments,-of $53,991,334. We adopted the process of writing off investments which cannot be looked upon as active. Payments therefore on their account cannot be deducted from the debt. For example, railway investments and the Quebec harbour investment have been regarded as unremunerative; but the fact remains that even if we take all the public works capital, all the railway capital, all the investments in railways and in the Quebec harbour, and the cost of the few items that still remain of the war, the whole payments down to 20th March last, only amount to $372,000,000. But here, in the face of a claim for a reduction of $138,000,000 in the Estimates, we have estimates calling for a total expenditure of $466,000,000, and if the railway guarantees given during the year as of March 20th, of $50,000,000 are added to the total expenditure for the year down to March 20th, would stand at $422,889,000. I do not think we are at all unreasonable in our demands under the circumstances. We now find ourselves in this situation. The Government have brought down estimates showing a saving of $138,000,000 and yet their total costs of operation down to the 20th of March, as nearly as I can make out amount to $422,889,000. Nevertheless in the face of that enormous paper saving the Government requires a substantially larger vote than the whole of last year's

expenditure. I quite understand the dilemma in which the Minister of Finance finds himself. Of course he is not going to put the closure through. speechtext: The increase was granted to this gentleman because of his important and very able services in the control of a very large expenditure.

Here is a department which is being reduced. A large number have been laid off during the past year because of the falling off in employment in the department. Having had the honour,

One of the first things that I learned on going into that department was that it was then in a position to lay off nearly 1,000 employees. I have nothing to say re-

garding the increase in salary for this officer; I do not remember being acquainted with the gentleman at all; but as regards the officers in general of that department, they were a very capable, able group of men. If there is any other which should be given the same sympathetic care, it is the department of Pensions, and I am sure the minister may feel quite certain that this party in this corner of the House-and I am sure the same is true of all parties in the House-will support him when he brings forward his Estimates for that department, so that the men who have returned from overseas may receive fair treatment. I am quite sure my hon. friend and the party with which he is associated, would not claim any particular economy in regard to that department because of the reductions.

Increases are given to seven of the ten officials in this vote, one increase amounting to $500. Why, therefore, should we make such enormous increases as we find in this estimate? A salary of $4,500 to-day is equivalent to $5,500 a couple of years ago, and will increase in value until wages strike the bottom. If the Government intend to economize they might very well start with the salaries of the civil servants, especially salaries as high as $4,500 a year. I have had very few minutes to look over the Estimates, but what we find in connection with this department is true in the case of nearly every other branch of the Civil Service. The Government, I submit, should begin with such salaries in any attempt to economize.

This increase of $500 is for the Supervisor of Expenditures. It is about the largest increase for the year, and a few moments ago I gave the reason for it. My hon. friend (Mr. Mewburn) suggested the appointment of a royal commission to inquire into the complaints and the needs of ex-service men. The practice up to the present has been to appoint a parliamentary committee every session; that, at least, has been done since my return from the Old Country. It has been deemed advisable to confine the inquiries of that committee within certain limits, and I have been of the opinion, as I think every member of the House has been, that it was a proper course to follow. As my hon. friend has said, it is somewhat difficult for special cases to be brought before the parliamentary committee, especially when the men concerned reside at any considerable distance from the Capital. But if the Government appointed a royal commission to travel, as is suggested, from one end of the country to the other, though it might be able to hear every special case on the spot, still thousands of cases would have to be examined, and the inconvenience would be so considerable as to render the process unsatisfactory. Altogether I do not think there could be any advantage in a royal commission, from the point of view of either the public or the returned man himself. I submit that as a consideration, although I do not want to say that I am opposed to the appointment of a royal commission. The parliamentary committee has dealt, in years gone by, with numberless special cases. I well remember, that there were brought

Supply-Re-Establishment
before the attention of a sub-committee, appointed by the parliamentary committee on Pensions and Re-Establishment, cases which were examined in the presence of the Chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners, two other commissioners, and some of the highest officials of the department. How could it be possible for a royal commission, which should travel from one end of the country to the other, to take all the officials of the departments along with them? How, for instance, could they have the Pension Commissioners with them all the time in Calgary, Vancouver, or Halifax during four, or five, or six months, as the case might be? I fancy it would take a long time to conduct this investigation, and the difficulties that impede the parliamentary committee would exist, perhaps in a larger measure, in the case of a royal commission such as is suggested. Most of the cases considered by the parliamentary committee at the last session of Parliament and the session before were, I think, satisfactorily solved. My hon. friend is conversant with the subject, and, as he has pointed out, there are a very large number of cases which ought to be submitted to some tribunal for a more exhaustive investigation. There is no doubt about that. In the few weeks that I have been at the head of the department, I have convinced myself, from the correspondence I have received, that there are many complaints amongst the returned men as regards their treatment, especially in connection with pensions.
I am not prepared to lay the blame at the door of the late Government for everything that has happened. This committee must remember one thing: A Board of Pension Commissioners has been created by a statute of this Parliament, and that statute provides that the decisions of the Board shall be final; there is no appeal to +lie minister, no appeal to the Governor in Council. The only tribunal to which the men who are not satisfied with an award may have recourse is a parliamentary committee, or in other words, Parliament itself. I have been two or three months at the head of this department, and I have not yet received any complaint as to the action of the parliamentary committee of last year. I do not know whether my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia (Mr. Mewburn) has heard of any complaints against that committee. I think the men have had every possible opportunity, through their various organizations of laying their whole case before the
committee, and the committee of last year was composed of men who had only in view the reconciling of the public interest with the interest of the returned men, because those two interests must be reconciled.
My hon. friend has referred to the special cases, those known as "problem" cases. Those cases exist in fairly large numbers throughout the country, such as tubercular cases. I am a medical man, and I would not declare offhand in the case of a soldier who has been gassed and discharged as 100 per cent fit, and who subsequently develops tuberculosis three years after his discharge, that the disease was not due to his war service, and I hardly think that any chest specialist would go that length. Those are cases which require the special attention of the committee and of this Parliament. Justice should be done to those men, and if any doubt should exist as to the cause of tuberculosis in any man who has seen actual war service in the trenches, and who has been gassed, he should be given the benefit of the doubt. I think that that was the policy of the late Government; I think it is the policy of this Government; and I think it would meet with the approval of every reasonable and humane man in Canada. The question is, how are you going to establish that such a disability, appearing subsequently, is due to war service?
How can those cases reach the parliamentary committee, or this House, if there is no appeal from the Pension Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I would point out that last year the question of these tubercular cases was gone into very fully by the parliamentary committee, and some reports which would be a credit to any country in the world were prepared and submitted regarding tubercular cases. I expect that this question will come before the committee again this year with a view, very likely, to more being done for these tubercular cases.

I am not disputing that at all. I am absolutely in favour of it, but if there is no appeal from the board, I cannot see how you can get a remedy unless the proposition is to amend the act. If that is the minister's proposition, it is well worth considering.
