Mr. Chairman, sitting
pretty close to the official Opposition I find myself somewhat in sympathy with the criticism they have offered in regard to these increases; with a lot of what they have said I find myself entirely out of sympathy. I am not going to take time now to tell about the faults and the wrongdoings of either of the old political parties; if I were to do so I think we would be here all night and all day to-morrow. I am thoroughly convinced, however, from what I have heard them say about each other that the Progressives should have been here several years ago-that is a fact of which I am thoroughly convinced.
I would like to say that I am very much disappointed that so many increases are asked for in the Estimates that have been brought down. It is very nice, indeed, that those engaged in the government employ as civil servants shall receive additions to their salaries, but what about those who are receiving very much less, who have to pay these increases? I felt when I came here-and many of my Progressive friends had the same feling-that we should be prepared to give every degree of credit to the Government if they were deserving of credit, and that we should also give credit to the official Opposition where it was deserved. I felt determined, when I went back to my constituents, that any degree of credit that was coming, either to the Government or to the Opposition, should be given them as honestly as I could give it. I considered that in that way I would be doing something towards the good government of the country, and the Government, knowing our attitude, I believe, would be more apt to do the right thing, but looking as we are, for retrenchment and economy, and finding these increases asked for which I cannot justify, I feel very much afraid that I shall not be able to say the good things I intended to say with reference to the Government and their economy. As the people in the West know that $5,000 per anum in Ontario, say in the city of Ottawa, will go as far as $7,000, or perhaps $8,000, in the West, I am inclined to think that, under present conditions, with	the economic
depression under which we are suffering, and the necessity for strictest economy, they will consider that such increases as have been asked for here are not justified.
Much has been said about the condition of the West, and I am not going to deal with it. It has been discussed at considerable length, but I assure you that what has been said has not been overdrawn. We are living in critical times. There has been such a keen competition between the different factions, and the different industries throughout the country, each striving to get what it could, without any thought as to the other fellow, that these industries have driven the agricultural classes pretty well to the wall, and if the crop this year should fail, I shudder to think of the result. I am afraid the industrial and commercial life of Canada would almost topple over like a house of cards.
I have been looking, and hoping, for the strictest economy in connection with the Civil Service. It is hard to get proof of many things I believe, but I think that a great many more officials are engaged than are required. While there are many who are giving efficient service, who are earning their money and are not getting any more than they should receive, on the other hand, there are men engaged in the Civil Service who are not required. How do you suppose the returned soldier who was placed in a position of want and need, would feel when he went into the Soldiers' Settlement Board in the city of Regina, was kept waiting two hours before he could see the party he wished to see, and observed twenty stenographers, not one of whom, during those two hours, handled the typewriter? He would get the impression -and I think many have the impression- that, while a large sum of money may have been expended, as has been pointed out here, in re-establishing returned soldiers and paying them pensions at figures that would seem to indicate that they have been better treated in Canada than in other countries-too much of the money has gone into administration, and too much to the officers rather than to the private soldiers. I would like to see an analysis of the figures, and see how much has been spent in administration, how much has gone to officers, and how much to private soldiers. I have met many private soldiers who, I am quite convinced, have not been fairly treated. I am not going to speak at length on this matter, but I do not feel like backing up the action of the minister or the Government in increasing salaries all along the line.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I quite appreciate the remarks which have been made by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Millar). I am also of the opinion that the strictest economy and retrenchment should



Supply-Re-Establishment
be practised in administration, not only in this department but in all other departments of the public service. It is true that in every department there is a considerable number of officials who are receiving somewhat high salaries, but I may be permitted to say to my hon. friend that those salaries are based on a classification which has been made. The salary attached to each particular class is fixed by the Civil Service Commission, or by the reclassification board employed by the late government for the purpose. This afternoon some remarks were made on the subject of the increase of $500 to the supervisor of expenditures, whose salary was already $4,500. The right hon. gentleman, in explanation given to the House, stated that these officials were not subject to the Civil Service Commission or rather, to be exact, that the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment did not fall under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. In a large measure that is true, but in so far as the civil government employees are concerned, they come under the supervision of the Civil Service Commission and in this particular instance the $500 which is asked for as an increase cannot be paid to Mr. Waddington, or the supervisor of expenditures, until it has been authorized by the Civil Service Commission, and that applies to all other officials whose salaries are under study and observation by the commission at the present time. As to the other officials, the increase is the regular increase provided for all officials-absolutely the same. As regards the promises and pledges made during the election campaign, my hon. friend is undoubtedly better posted than I am. Though it was my privilege to cover a large part of Canada during the last campaign, I never heard either the leader of the Government or any gentleman associated with him on the platform making threats of the kind that have been referred to. I cannot, of course, speak for those who delivered public addresses in my absence. The manifesto of a certain gentleman, who stood as Liberal candidate in British Columbia, has been quoted in this House. I am not in a position to answer for him. I am not, moreover, exactly informed in the subject, and, perhaps, other hon. gentlemen are not.

What about the official Liberal handbook which I hold in my hand?
rMr. Bfiland.]

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I explained before six o'clock to my hon. friend that it is quite evident to-day, after recent conventions of the Veterans, that the sentiment of the latter, and the veterans at large in Canada, is unalterably opposed to the payment of a cash bonus.
The Great War Vet-eans' Association was never in favour of paying a cash bonus; it was a little body of returned men headed by a man called Flynn.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend has been, for a long time, a member of this House, and I know he wants to be fair; but if he sat with us in the parliamentary committee two years ago when that coim mittee convened at the Museum, he will remember that, outside of Mr. Flynn or bis followers, three or four gentlemen representing very important bodies of returned men submitted to the committee a definite plan for the payment of a cash bonus. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) was present, and he will remember that it was a well-elaborated plan. It was, indeed, an attractive plan, but at that time it did not carry with the committee or with Parliament. Since then, as everyone is aware, it has developed that the veterans, with the exception of a very few, are opposed to the payment of a cash bonus. If I am not mistaken, listening to the hon. gentleman who leads the Government (Mr. Mackenzie Ring), I took it that his idea was not so much that a cash bonus should be paid to the returned men, as that our duty towards the returned men would be measured by the ability of the country to pay; that he would go as far as the financial resources of the country would warrant. That is what I took from the remarks of the present Prime Minister all through the campaign while it was my privilege to accompany him. I do not know why my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), who leads the Opposition so ably, should attempt to make a little political capital out of this thing.
1 sat for three years on the parliamentary committee as a member representing the then Opposition in this House, I had associated with me, a number of Liberal members, and not on one occasion did we seek to gain a particle of political advantage out of a proposition that we might have made at the time, not only in the country, but on the floor of this House. Hon. gentlemen who sat in the previous House, many of whom I see here, will remember that when the then hon. member for London, Mr. Cronyn, presented to this House the report of the committee, I for

Supply-Re-Establishment
one rose in my seat to concur in it, and it was adopted unanimously. Who would deny that, such an opportunity being offered to me, I could not have availed myself of it to propose something that I knew the government could not carry out. I never did that. Why? Because I think it is really criminal, in the case of returned men and their cause, that we should seek any political advantage. It is beyond doubt that, in a heated campaign, some men will publish something that may attract a few votes to them. That has happened undoubtedly amongst some of the Liberal candidates, and who can say, without fear of contradiction, that some of my right hon. friend's friends have not, on some occasion, resorted to the same tactics. I am quite sure they have. But we are here to study the important problem of re-establishment, as we have been engaged in doing in previous sessions, and let us examine this question without allowing ourselves to be biased by political or partisan inclinations. That is my view of the subject. I think I have given the committee, in all good faith and sincerity, the reasons why these salaries should be voted. Whether it be the desire of the committee that they should be passed, is another matter.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that he believed a great majority ofj the returned soldiers were unalterably opposed to a cash bonus. Is that correct?
Mr.'BELAND: Yes, that is what I said.

I am afraid the hon. gentleman has in mind an indiscriminate cash bonus. Will he also say that he believes the returned soldier is not in favour of a cash bonus which is dependent in amount upon length of service?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am not aware of any such resolutions being adopted by any of the veterans' organizations. The returned men have submitted a number of suggestions to this Government, as they have to the late government. These suggestions in due course will be submitted to the parliamentary committee that is shortly to be appointed for the purpose of studying the important questions of re-establishment generally, the treatment of special or problem cases, the problem of amputation cases, the insurance feature of re-establishment, the treatment of patients generally, the granting of pensions and the care of the disabled soldier. Upon all these subjects we have received a number of suggestions,
and they will be studied in due course by a committee that will be appointed. My personal opinions on the subject are well known. Anything which can be done on behalf of the returned men and which is compatible with the resources of the country, I for one am in favour of doing.

I quite believe my hon. friend is sincere in his remarks; but when he -states that neither the leader of the Government (Mr. Mackenzie King), nor any one of the men who were associated with him, ever on the platform spoke in favour of the $2,000 gratuity, or anything verging upon that-that is about what I understood him to say-I think, perhaps, he is a little mistaken, because I hold in my hand an article which I remember reading at the time during my campaign in my constituency stating that when the leader of the present' Government spoke in Port Arthur he begged the Liberals of Fort William to bring out a candidate against me, a thing which they did not do. When he spoke there, he had accompanying him Colonel Thompson, a personal friend of mine, a gentleman for whom I have a great deal of respect. Colonel Thompson spoke in the presence of the present Prime Minister, because he spoke right after the Prime Minister. According to the Fort William Times Journal of November 11, this is what Colonel Thompson said:
Colonel Thompson spoke briefly, as he said the previous speakers had handled the questions of the day so completely there was little for him to say. He pledged the loyalty of the returned man to the country, declaring at the same time that the $2,000 bonus was not more than he deserved, in view of the high wages paid during the war to the men who remained in the industries. But the returned men were loyal, etc.
And he goes on with other remarks. Now, I admit that that is not an express endorsation of the demand for the $2,000 bonus; but if it is not an implied support of that demand, particularly in view of the fact that the Liberal party's platform pledged itself to the grant, then I do not quite know what it is. The leader of the Government (Mr. Mackenzie King) was on the platform when Colonel Thompson made this speech, and he had spoken a few minutes before Colonel Thompson did. In fact, just before the account of Colonel Thompson's speech is a report of my hon. friend's remarks, and he certainly had at that time an opportunity to put himself on record as being opposed to the $2,000 grant, just as I did. I remember well
Supply-Re-Establishment

making a speech which was used against me in my election, because I had taken a stand against the grant. May I say to my hon. friends on the left, before I sit down, that some of them have been unfairly critical of hon. members in this corner of the House because they have thought it necessary to consider this question. Hon. gentlemen on our left speak as though we were wasting time. I presume, however, that when we come to the tariff they will take up the plank of the Liberal platform and deal with it from their point of view because it happens to suit their purpose. Just at the moment the party at this end of the Chamber think that the question of the grant to the soldiers is one that can fairly be discussed, and I think that if my hon. friends on the left of us can discuss any question that suits them, we should be able to do the same. I may say that I ran against a gentleman who supported the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), and although I have nothing to say against him personally, many of the friends who worked in his interest carried on against me as lying and slanderous a campaign as was ever conducted against a man in any fight in the country. I do not see, therefore, why we should be chided because once in a while we spend a little time discussing this matter, which was embodied in the plank of the Liberal party's platform.

Before six ocloelc, Mr. Chairman, I drew your attention to the fact that the discussion was out of order. We are considering a matter of voting salaries to pay nine employees in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. I can quite understand that it may be a pleasant occupation to hold political inquests, and I could do a little inquesting myself under this head if I cared to do so. I submit to my hon. friend (Mr. Manion), however, that the whole discussion of the bonus is out of order under this head, and I ask for your ruling, Mr. Chairman.

May I speak to this
question before you give your decision, Mr. Chairman? I think that on these Estimates any part of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment vote comes up for consideration, and to my mind the question of the $2,000 bonus is certainly a part of this whole question. The grant was claimed by a large percentage of returned soldiers headed by Flynn, and it is still claimed by many; and I repeat that the question was used against me in my own

constituency. So long as it is a claim on the part of the returned soldiers in the country, it is, in my opinion, just as right to discuss the bonus as it is to consider the wages of the men who carry out the re-establishment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The member for
Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has asked for a ruling on the relevancy of the discussion respecting a bonus to returned soldiers. In my opinion there is very much ground for the position taken by the hon. member, and I feel that the discussion has exceeded reasonable bounds. I do not think that the remarks of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) are entirely relevant to the subject before the committee, but this being my first day in the Chair, I have been inclined to allow some latitude to discussion. Perhaps I should have been within the strict interpretation of the rules had I called hon. members to order before, but the discussion, I think, is now distinctly out of order.

In view of the fact that there is no item in the Estimates for soldier appropriations, it would be useful to the committee, Mr. Chairman, if you would suggest under what item we might discuss this subject.
There are various ways in Which my right hon. friend can bring the matter before the House. He can do so by way of private member's resolution in condemnation of the Government.
But in committee.

I submit that if on any item before the House we are to wander over the whole field of political inquesting, we shall never get through with the business of the session. I have a good deal of sympathy with the attitude my right hon. friend has taken, and the leader of the Government is perhaps in a rather difficult position in giving an explanation; but I submit that this is not the proper place in which to discuss this question. I want to see the business of the House proceed and the minister in charge of the department get his estimates through, with such reasonable explanations as the House is entitled to have.

I do not think the minister has given an explanation on one question I asked before, and I shall put the question again as clearly as I can. The department last year had twenty-five clerks and officers, and sixteen clerks have been

Supply-Re-Establishment
discharged because there was no more work for them. At least, that is what we infer from the Estimates: to use the words in the Estimates, "the position is not required." The Government has retained nine of these officers, and they are the highest paid. Surely some of the highly-paid executive officers could have been dispensed with if the Minister could discharge two-thirds of the staff. The answer suggested by my hon. friend, that the Civil Re-establishment Department includes the Pension Board, does not affect this question at all; the Pension Board carry on all their business with their own staff and with their own appropriation, and all that the minister has to do is to act as a medium of approach between the Pension Board and Parliament. His staff has very little, if anything, to do with the Pension Board administration. We should therefore have an explanation as to why the Government cannot dispense with some of the highly paid executive staff in conjunction with the sixteen clerks for whom there is now no work.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The officials for whom the salaries are being asked administer the department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. At the present time this department comprises in round numbers, not twenty-nine, but five thousand employees in the different units throughout the country from Vancouver to Halifax. In Ottawa we have some eleven hundred employees, and we have units also in Vancouver, Calgary, Winnipeg, London, Ont., Toronto, Montreal and Halifax.
As regards these sixteen clerical positions not required, we are not dispensing with these men. We thought they would probably be required, but have found that they will not be required for this year. Perhaps my hon. friend was absent from the House before six o'clock when I stated that a number of the higher officials are being' dispensed with. I cited the case of an official in Toronto drawing a salary of $5,000 a year whose services would terminate on the last day of this month. If I am not mistaken, his name is Mr. Coulthard, in charge of the surgical appliances branch.
I am informed by the officials of the department that he will not be replaced. I also cited the case of an engineer in Montreal, drawing a salary of over $3,000, whose services have already been dispensed with, and there are other cases. I could have supplied full information to the committee and had the deputy minister with me had I known that these questions would be
raised. My hon. friend may rest assured that it is not only the officials drawing small salaries, that are being dispensed with, but, proportionately, an equal number of the higher officials.
Not in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
If my hon. friend were
minister of this department he could realize that these officials are actually required, to carry out in an efficient manner the work of the department all over the country, and unless my worthy predecessor thinks these men should be dispensed with, I doubt whether we should let them go, at the present time at all events. It was represented to me that these men are necessary for the efficient carrying out of the work of the department.

Starting with the
lower salaried, officials and going up the list, there is first an increase of $40; one of $60, and three of $120, the last one being an increase from $3,240 to $3,360. Then we have a rather large jump in the salary of the Supervisor of Expenditures, from $4,500 to $5,000. I should like to ask the minister whether the Supervisor of Expenditures, has any particular educational or technical qualifications to justify that increase. What is the explanation for this jump in his salary? An increase of $120 seems quite reasonable, but it almost looks as though it were a case of the higher the salary the higher the increase which is really quite a familiar thing to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It will be to my eternal honour that some explanations of mine have drawn into the discussion in this committee the first lady member of the House. I hope that I shall be successful in answering the question which she has so gracefully asked. The increase is always, I think, based on the amount of the salary, and is regulated by the Civil Service Commission. In the case of a man drawing a salary of $4,500, I would think that if an increase was granted at all, it should be $500. In the case of the next man down the list, who is now receiving $3,240, the increase is proportionately less, $120. Lower down the list, as my hon. friend from Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) has pointed out, the increases drop from $60 to $40. I would repeat that no increase in salary in these eases can be granted unless it is approved by the Civil Service Commission.
Not in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes, in this case. There can be no increase in salary unless author-

Supply-Re-Establishment
ized under the Civil Service Act, which means, by the Civil Service Commission. Answering the question by my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) this afternoon, Mr. Waddington was appointed after competitive examination three years ago.
Is the Supervisor of Expenditures working on a graded salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am not in a position to give that information at present, but I shall be glad to do so when the Estimates of the department are up.

I think raising a man's salary in this way is a bad precedent to establish. I have a great interest in the returned men, and anything the minister may do for them will have my sincere sympathy and support. I was inspired to suggest this afternoon that a royal commission be appointed to deal with these special cases, so that the returned men who had grievances could appear before the commission as it travelled over the country and lay their cases before them. I might mention one particular case, that of a fireman on one of the railways. He went overseas, came back and was discharged, and since has been invalided. I am sorry to say he had to be sent to an asylum, and now he has a seizure every day or two and is not fit to carry on any work. He has a wife and child, and nothing to support them. The D.S.C.R. refuses to support him. They say that under the Act they cannot do anything for him. It is such cases as this that the royal commission could take up. I have the honour, Mr. Chairman, to be a supporter of the right hon. Arthur Meighen-
Order.

-a man possessed of distinguished qualities, a man who has both backbone and ability; a man who is highly regarded in all parts of this Dominion. I may say that at a meeting at which the right hon. Arthur Meighen was to speak-
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that while it has always been the custom under the items of the Estimates pertaining to civil government to discuss the general policy of the department concerned, he is, I think, travelling rather far afield. We have spent a good deal of time on this resolution, and I would ask the hon. member to deal particularly with the matter

under discussion as found on page 113 of the Estimates.

I am not transgressing
the rules any more than other hon. members did, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Then if I may not go ahead I will take my seat.

I am not just clear in my mind as to what jurisdiction these particular salaries come under. It has been pointed out by the leader of the Opposition that they do not come under Civil Service Commission; yet the minister has referred to increases which are granted under the rules of that body. I am at sea as to what those rules are, as regards maximum salary and so on. The increases asked for cannot be justified by the increased duties of the officers concerned, because sixteen clerks have been dispensed with, as well as other officials; so that the work of the department must surely be lessened. Nor can the increase be based on the cost of living, because reports issued by the Department of Labour go to show that the cost of living has come down in all branches. It seems to me that the more serious part of this question has not yet been touched on. There is an increase of but $960 in respect of six positions, but there is a precedent being established which may affect a great many positions in the gift of the Government. The Minister of Railways, through his heads of departments, will have to convince some of the railroad men that they should accept lower wages in order that freight rates may be reduced. If the principle involved in the increases now proposed is adopted in one case and not in another, some difficulty may result. If these increases are put through, what about the principles of economy that were preached before the election? The Government would be well advised to forego any such increases as are now proposed.

I have been waiting
patiently throughout this discussion to hear some justification of these increases. If the efficiency of the minister's department is going to be proportionately increased by adding $500 to the salary of one employee, $120 to the salaries of several others, $60 and $40 in other cases, I should offer no objection, because I do not believe we can have in any of these departments too high

Supply-Railways
a degree of efficiency. But that has not been established by any explanation made by the hon. minister. It has not been shown that there is any logical connection between the increases asked for 9 p.m. and the reduction in the total personnel. If additional duties or responsibilities were to devolve upon remaining employees because of a reduction in the numbers of the staff, we could reconcile ourselves to increases, provided, as appears from these Estimates, there is a considerable reduction in the total amount required by the department. I was elected, as was almost everyone sitting on this side of the House, on a platform of strict economy.
Not including the hon. members to your extreme right.

Oh, no. Mr. Chairman, I come from a portion of the country where in municipality after municipality the farmers, to the extent of seventy-five per cent of the population, are unable to pay their provincial taxes. Furthermore, in order to redeem that portion of the country, in order to make it a national asset instead of a national liability, those farmers have assumed a burden amounting to $5,000,000 for the purpose of irrigation. In order to put that country on its proper footing they have assumed an indebtedness that it will take nearly all this generation of farmers in the district to discharge. I cannot go back and face my people there if I vote for increases which are not justified by efficiency or by some other good and sufficient reason. There is a large decrease in the total amount asked for this department. I believe that the minister is heartily in favour of doing all he can for the returned men, and I would like to stand behind him. But I would like a further justification of the increases asked by this vote.

The Minister has said that under the rules of the Civil Service Commission the maximum salary of employees now getting $4,500 is $5,000. The Estimates, however, show that that rule does not apply in other departments. I do not think that is the scale adopted by the Civil Service Commission.

Item agreed to.
Department o£ Railways and Canals- salaries, $191,970 ; Contingencies, $29,500.
Sir HENRY DRAYTON; Explain.

['The Minister has said that under the rules of the Civil Service Commission the maximum salary of employees now getting $4,500 is $5,000. The Estimates, however, show that that rule does not apply in other departments. I do not think that is the scale adopted by the Civil Service Commission.']

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution carry?
Mr. MEI'GHEN: One moment. Surely the Minister of Railways is not going to ask that all his civil government estimates go through without any explanation, particularly when that minister permitted an ambiguous, almost meaningless, assertion of policy in the Speech from the Throne to come before Parliament to be voted on without any details as to what the intention of the Government was, and after a promise from the Prime Minister that the desired explanation would be given. We ought to have had that explanation even before being called upon to pass the Address. Surely it is now the duty of the minister to tell the House what -the policy of the Government in relation to the railways is before we are asked to vote the civil government estimates providing for the salaries of the officers of the department. For example, would it not be interesting to know whether the Intercolonial railway is to be taken out from the management of the national railways and placed again under the Department of Railways and Canals as was promised by certain members supporting the Government? Is that promise to be carried out? If so we may 'be required to vote these estimates and more, because the railway department will have more to do then than it has to-day, and we will have a lot of questions as to who are going to be necessary and who are not. These estimates may be necessary if the Intercolonial is really going back under the administration of the Department of Railways but may not be necessary if the administration of that railway stays where it is. Now is the time, when we are entering upon the consideration of the railway estimates, to know what the railway policy of the Government is. I hope the desired explanation will not be deferred again. I hope we shall not be asked to vote money from the Treasury to carry out the railway policy of the Government without knowing what that policy is.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. C. KENNEDY (Minister of Railways and Canals) :
speechtext:
My right hon.
friend the Prime Minister is not more anxious-

I beg my hon. friend's pardon?
Mr. KENNEDY (Essex); I should say the ex-Prime Minister; we have been so accustomed to refer to my right hon. friend as the Prime Minister that I for the moment forgot the change that has taken place. I want to tell my right hon. friend
Supply-Railways

that I am just as anxious to make a statement to the House as he is to hear it. I hope, however, he will agree with me that in order to present an intelligent statement it is necesary that we should be in possession of all the facts and figures essential for the purposes of comparison when considering the main Estimates. The railroads that are under the jurisdiction of the Government have to make their returns at the end of the year and these returns should be embodied in the railway statement. They have not yet been submitted to the department. I am awaiting these statistics and they cannot come too soon; I am doing everything I can to hurry them up. Then I shall be glad indeed to make a statement of the Government's railway policy as far as I can and explain the transactions of the past year. Tonight we are simply called upon to discuss the civil government estimates of the department. In so far as the main Estimates are concerned it will be necessary to have the story of the past year's operations before we can discuss them intelligently. All that I am now asking, Mr. Chairman, is that we go on with the estimates of civil government.

In the Speech from the Throne it is stated that the policy of the Government is to co-ordinate the different railway properties that belong to the Canadian people, and it does seem to me that before being asked to take up any railway estimates at all we might very well have from the Minister of Railways a statement of just what the Government means by the use of the word "co-ordination". The word is susceptible of a great many meanings. It may mean just what this Government believes to be the proper policy, it may mean many other things; and it does seem to me that the Minister of Railways ought, before going on with any part of his Estimates to give to the committee a statement of exactly what the Government means; how they propose to manage the different properties; what they propose to do with the properties now managed by the Grand Trunk Board, and what they propose to do with the properties having regard to the management under the board of which Mr. Hanna is the head. These are matters that in no way depend upon the annual reports to which the minister has just referred. We on this side urge that that statement be given to the committee, that the committee be told in clear terms exactly what the policy of the Government is-either that

or that the items we are now asked to consider stand until that statement has been given.

The hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat was Minister of Railways for two or three months just before the out-going government went to the people. Nobody knows better than he, therefore, that in so far as these estimates are concerned the question of co-ordination does not bear on them at all. These are civil government estimates, there is nothing in them that will be affected by the meaning of the term "coordination." I have told his leader and I have told the committee that before the main estimates are brought in I will submit a statement giving in full the policy of this Government. To-night I am asking that the civil government estimates be taken up and it is for the committee to decide whether they care to do so or not.

It seems to me that the question as to how the Government proposes to handle the railway properties is one that has direct reference to the items we are now asked to consider. These officers for whom salaries are sought will have to do with the management of the railway properties; and whether these properties are to be managed as they are now, or managed by two boards, or whether we are to follow the advice of the member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) and the member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and have another management of the Intercolonial-these are all matters that surely bear direct reference to the estimates we are now asked to consider. The two hon. members referred to have laid it down as a part of the Confederation pact that the Intercolonial railway must be taken away from the management of any of these boards. That must be done they say, in order to carry out what preceded Confederation, and to give effect to what I understood the member for Cumberland to say was contained in Section 142 of the British North America Act.
Section 145.

Very well. Section 145 of the British North America Act-that in order to carry out its terms we must place this road back under government and political control, and with that control must go the regulation of the rates without any regard to either the cost of operation or the judgment of the Board of Railway Commissioners. It does seem to me therefore that the whole question of

Supply-Railways
the administration of the Railway Department is one which depends upon how these properties are going to be handled, and it is surely a reasonable request that we either have the statement asked for, or that these items shall stand until that statement is presented by the minister.

I have again to say to my hon. friend that he simply wishes to anticipate the statement that will be made when I am in possession of the facts that bear upon it and when the right time comes it will be presented. There are many questions arising in connection with the subject and everyone will have ample opportunity to present his views when that time comes; but such a discussion to-night is entirely out of place. In the debate in the Speech from the Throne the leader of the Government told my hon. friend perhaps the one thing he is most concerned about and that is that there is to be one control. That will be dealt with at the right time, and to-night I do not think it is out of the way to refer to the discussion that took place when the railway estimates were before the House on former occasions. If the hon. gentleman will refer to the discussion a year ago, when the hon. Dr. Reid had charge of railways and canals, he will find that we discussed the civil government estimates without the statement of the minister, and I am only asking the House to do what has been the practice in the past, with the full assurance that at the right time, and in the very near future, I will be able to give the hon. gentleman the full information which he desires.

The items
we are asked to consider are not urgent. If they were, there might be something in the claim that is now made by the minister. Last year, when the House was asked to consider these same items, under the conditions that have been stated by the minister, we were on into the middle of April. None of these items is required. The amount provided for in the votes is not required at the present time, and no interests will suffer by delay. If it were a question of the money not being available to pay the items at the present time, it seems to me the minister would be justified in making the request which he has made to-night, but, in view of the fact that the money is not required, it seems to me that the request we make on this side of the House, that these matters be allowed to stand until we are able to take up the whole question, is a reasonable one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suggest that the same objection might be raised to any item that is not urgent. All the items in the Estimates are urgent. We are anxious to advance business, and, therefore, the criticism is not a strong one. We are proceeding in the same way as Parliament proceeded in former years. I do not hesitate to say that if hon. gentlemen think this item should not be hurried along too much, I will offer no objection, and I will advise my hon. friend the Minister of Railways to consent. But the same thing might be said for every department. You might say "It is not urgent, what is the hurry?" There is no particular hurry, except that all business must be put through.

Surely there is this difference between this department and any other department; that the minister himself has stated that there is due the House a statement, which was not only promised in the Speech from the Throne, but in the remarks made by the Prime Minister himself upon the Address. There is that difference between this department and any other department that might be considered. In that respect I do not think, as the hon. Minister of Finance has said, that it is exactly on all fours with any other department and the objection that we urge in this connection could not be urged with the same force against any other department. The question of urgency is an incident. It is not the objection on which we are asking for delay. We are asking for delay, not because the items are not urgent, but because we have not the statement that has been promised to the House by the minister, and for that reason we request that the items be allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think there is material difference between the procedure now and the procedure in_ other sessions? The statement of the minister is due, but, it is not always brought in. Whether promised in the Speech or not, the statement has to accompany the main Estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals, and always did, and that is the practice now. However, if the hon. gentleman thinks it is desirable that this item be held over, I do not wish to suggest that it should be pressed.

We certainly ask to have it stand. As to the railway policy, there is uncertainty. Hon. gentlemen opposite would not dispute that there is uncer-
Supply-Privy Council

tainty as to what the Government propose to do on major questions of public policy. There is uncertainty, and doubt, even in the Speech from the Throne itself. No one on this side of the House knows what is going to be done. We do not know what are to he the responsibilities of the Department of Railways. I do not know whether hon. gentlemen opposite do or not, but I venture to suggest over half of them do not, and I venture also to suspect that at least a third of them expect something to be done that is not going to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a good reason for objecting.

Unquestionably there is doubt as to the railway policy. Now, I put it to the Minister of Finance: Is there any subject, is there any department, as to the policy of which there is no uncertainty on the part of this Government? If there is one I should like to take up the civil estimates of that department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend would say there is none.
Yes, and perhaps the hon. gentleman will admit the truth of that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let us take up my Estimates. They are practically the same as the Estimates of the right hon. gentleman last year.

I expect there is no policy with regard to the hon. gentleman's estimates, so that perhaps we can take them up.
Item stands.
Privy Council, Salaries,	$44,810
Contingencies	 10,000

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The bases of this estimate are the figures that my hon. friend caused to be inserted last year. There are no Increases in the staff, and there are no increases in any of the salaries, excepting those that are statutory.
I see there is an extra clerk required. The minister tells us that the increases here are statutory. Is that one clerk a statutory increase, or how is that?
He is trading an office boy for a private secretary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think it is a private secretary.	[DOT]

How many private
secretaries has the minister? All those

formerly employed are apparently to be
employed again, except the office boy, and I do not really recall who that was. I cannot remember any office boy. And thp next is "allowance to private secretary $600". That is the ordinary allowance. In place of those two items, there is to be another private secretary at $3,600 and another assistant at $3,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the amount the hon. gentleman just mentioned of $600 was the amount voted in addition to the regular allowance of a clerk who served as a private secretary. That was adopted last session because my right hon. friend had a private secretary appointed as a clerk, and gave him the additional allowance of $600. Under the new Civil Service regulations, the appointment to the staff is made at the salary named in the estimates, no additional allowance being given to the official as private secretary.
That is correct, but it means an additional cost to the country of $5,610. Why not do it in the old way and save the country $5,610?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend will recall that there are two departments-Privy Council and the Department of External Affairs. I think he had control of only the one when he was Prime Minister. At the present time the office of President of the Privy Council has been consolidated with that of the Prime Minister, a saving of $10,000 being effected thereby. That has imposed an additional duty on the Prime Minister, and under the circumstances, it seemed permissible to allow him an extra private secretary. We save $10,000 by not having a separate portfolio, and all we add is a little extra for a private secretary.

I do not think that explanation will go. There was more under the Prime Minister before. The Mounted Police Department was under him, and I think there was some other department as well that is not now under the hon. gentleman. It is true the Presidency of the Privy Council is held now by the Minister of External Affairs; but the management of the Privy Council is merely a duty in Council; it is not a duty involving administrative functions particularly at all, not at all events since the mounted police, who formerly were under that department, and the Department of Health, have been moved out. I think there is, perhaps, one port-

Supply-External Affairs
folio less in the present Government than in the previous Government, but I think my calculation is correct that there are two more than in the Government which administered affairs during the last session of this House. There is an increase of about $20,000. The diminution is only over the government that was formed in the month of September, 1921; consequently, over what has prevailed substantially for a long time back, instead of there being a diminution, there is an increase, and I may say that I am not very hopeful that even this saving tof $10,000 will last very long. How many private secretaries are there? I do not see how more could be utilized; I do not know of any cause of more being utilized. I managed to keep those we had fairly busy, but I do not see how any minister could utilize any more.

Before the Prime
Minister replies, might I make an observation? One of the duties of private members on the Government side of the House is to listen attentively. Their work can be rendered much easier and much pleasanter for themselves, if Prime Minister, exPrime Minister, Ministers of the Crown and ex-Ministers of the Crown would speak in an audible voice.
Would the hon. member kindly tell us who the two additional secretaries are?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Beaudry is private secretary, and Mr. Talbot is assistant secretary.
Would the Prime Minister be good enough to tell us whether these private secretaries have been approved by the Civil Service Commission, or is this the extension of a little patronage on his part?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Civil
. Service Commission have approved their appointment in accordance with the regular method prescribed.

Item agreed to.
Civil Government-External Affairs-salaries and contingencies, $110,030.
['The Civil\n. Service Commission have approved their appointment in accordance with the regular method prescribed.']

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is a change of
one in the number of clerks; but with that exception, the amounts asked for are identical with what was asked for last year by the then Prime Minister when he was in charge of the Department of External Affairs. The only increases are those which are allowed by statute.

There seems
to be 100 per cent increase in private secretaries again. There was one private secretary before, and we now have two private secretaries. Is there a boom in private secretaries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If there is
any explanation needed in that regard, it is simply that the Estimates, as now presented, state exactly the position in which the clerk is employed. I am informed that in previous sessions a vote had been taken under the designation "secretary clerk," and the official having that position would fill the position of private secretary. I have tried to make it plain that the positions which these officials are intended to fill are those of private secretaries.

I am afraid
the Prime Minister should look at his Estimates for he is not getting rid of his secretary clerks. There were three secretary clerks before, and there are three this year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad
my hon. friend has mentioned that. It illustrates one of the difficulties set in the way of the Government under the working of the Civil Service Commission. My right hon. friend had a couple of very estimable gentlemen as his private secretaries. Under the working of the Civil Service regulations both of these gentlemen have to be retained in the Department of External Affairs at the salaries which they were then receiving, very high salaries, one being $3,800 and the other $4,000. I think it is obvious to hon. members that it could hardly be expected that an incoming Prime Minister should take over the private secretaries of the outgoing Prime Minister. Under these circumstances, it has been necessary to retain in the Department of External Affairs at the high salaries mentioned, the gentlemen who were secretaries to my right hon. friend. I might explain that one of these gentlemen has since been transferred by the Civil Service Commission to another department of the Government, a department for which he is well suited, and I hope that before long it will be possible to have the other gentleman also transferred to some other department, but under the working of the Civil Service Act as it is to-day, the Prime Minister is obliged to keep both of these gentlemen on the permanent staff at the salaries mentioned in the Estimates. I think both of them are splendid men, have filled their

Supply-External Affairs
positions with credit to themselves and have rendered real service to the country. It is a misfortune that we are restricted in the manner we are in the matter of making transfers.

Practically all the officials
in this branch down to the last four have their salaries increased, and strange to say, those who can least afford a reduction, namely, three confidential messengers and one messenger clerk, have their salaries reduced. The three confidential messengers suffer a loss of $180, and one messenger-clerk a loss of $120. It seems strange that those who get the larger salaries should be increased, while those with smaller allowances are cut down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is a matter regulated entirely by the Civil Service regulations. There are many aspects of the work of that body that are difficult of understanding and appreciation, and this would appear to be one of them. In regard to any decreases, unless there has been a transference of some clerk at a higher salary to some other department, which has necessitated the bringing in of another at a lower salary. I cannot see that there is anything to indicate that anyone has been reduced.
I appreciate the increases, because they are statutory; but surely there is nothing that compels you to reduce the salary of the lowest paid men.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What has
taken place is this. One high paid confidential messenger has been transferred to another department, and instead of bringing into the office another man at a similar salary, a messenger has been brought in as a junior who will have to work his way up.
What about the three confidential messengers? Have they all been transferred, or are they new messengers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is one new one, but the others were there when my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) was in the department.
I can understand the explanation regarding one, but not the four.

I owe it to the Prime Minister to confirm the principle which he expounded as regards secretaries. Efficient secretaries cannot be obtained if at the expiration of the term of office of their

minister they are to be merely turned out and let loose on the world. Consequently, it has been a rule that they shall be given the salary that they had before, without the secretarial allowance, and in so far as these Estimates provide for that, I commend rather than criticise them. I am not clear, however, as to how that was effected. I understand that my secretary, who was with me a considerable time, is going to the Interior Department, where certainly he can render his best service, and therefore there need be no provision for him here. But as regards the others, I see that $4,000 for one was voted last year, while this year there are two, one at $3,800 and one at $3,000. It may be that he is accepting a lower salary; if so I make no comment at the time. But still there appears to be another secretary, that is to say, there are two instead of one. In other words, there are two for the office of External Affairs and two for the office of the President of the Privy Council. I am afraid my hon. friend will not be able to get out of his office for secretaries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If my right hon. friend was able to get out of his office I shall not have any difficulty in getting out of mine, because I have the same number of secretaries as he had, I think he had the same number of persons acting as secretaries though they may not have been so designated. The only difference between himself and myself is that I have designated the office of secretary as such. It is quite true that I have a secretary attached to the office of the Privy Council, and also to the office of External Affairs, but as my right hon. friend knows, External Affairs appropriation covers also the requirements of the Prime Minister's office, and I do not think that anyone in this House will for a moment think it extravagant to ask for two secretaries for the responsible position of Prime Minister.

Certainly not, and I do not want to appear to dispute the word of the Prime Minister; but I cannot make his statement harmonize with the estimates. There are two secretaries provided for here in about the sixth item in the estimate. That is clear. Then going back to the Privy Council estimates, we find there are two more, or four in all. Now, I do not think that four secretaries can be efficiently used, but even supposing that they can,
I do not understand the explanation that these are simply officers who formerly acted

Supply-High Commissioner
as secretaries and are now being only named as such. If so, the Prime Minister should be able to point out where there is a reduction from last year's estimate in lieu of the men who acted as clerks last year. A man may have served as clerk last year, getting $600 extra as secretary. Well, show where he goes off as clerk, in order that we may understand why he appears again as secretary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is hardly fair when he seeks to imply that there are four secretaries for this one office. As I explained a moment ago, two departments of the Government have been brought under one minister, and I cannot agree with the leader of the Opposition when he says that there are no duties attaching to the office of President of the Privy Council. During all the time that he was Prime Minister he had four secretaries but he had also a separate minister holding the position of President of the Council, and that minister had his staff with him. He had his secretaries, and evidently there was work then for them to do. There is work to be done to-day, and it is a very considerable work, as my right hon. friend would know if he had acted as President of the Privy Council. I appreciate the fact that he was not President of the Council and therefore cannot be aware of the work attached to the office. The President of the Privy Council found it necessary to have the staff I ask for here, and I confess that I find it absolutely necessary myself.

I quite agree with the
remarks of the leader of the Opposition regarding the hardships suffered by secretaries who on the expiration of the term of office of their ministers are thrown out of employment. Is it the aim of the Government on this occasion to find work for such secretaries at the salaries that they would have drawn, with the $600 secretarial allowance deducted?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There again, it is not a matter so much of Government policy as what the Civil Service Commission will permit. There are a number of positions in the Civil Service to which men may be appointed at the instance of the Commission. So far as it is possible to do so, the Government is trying to take care of the secretaries of gentlemen who held portfolios in the late government. For instance, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) has retained
the secretary of his predecessor at exactly the same salary, and proposes to treat him in exactly the same way. That has not been possible in all departments, but we have endeavoured to look after those members of the service who were secretaries and to see that they receive the salaries that would be equivalent to what they earned previously in the departments. I think that a man who has served as an efficient private secretary to a minister of the Crown is likely to make the very best type of civil servant; he is apt to have much larger experience and wider information than any clerk, of the work of the Government departments except in special fields ; and I should like very much if some way could be found to retain men who have given service to the country, not by day only but also by night, year in and year out, and who at the time of change of administration might otherwise not be retained in their offices. It cannot all be done in a day, however.

On the whole, I think
.the Government have acted fairly with the secretaries of the late ministers. I do not know that that statement can be applied absolutely, but speaking generally I think they have acted fairly. I simply want to understand the vote. I think I understand by the last statement of the Prime Minister that he has two secretaries as President of the Privy Council and two secretaries as Minister of External Affairs, making four secretaries in all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I would state it in this way. I have one secretary as President of the Privy Council; he has an assistant. I have one secretary as Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs, and he has an assistant. As my right hon. friend knows, and this should be remembered, the difference between the office of the Prime Minister and that of other departments of the Government is that mos't of the work is necessarily carried on by the secretaries, not by a staff as in the case of other departments. Practically, the immediate personnel of the Prime Minister's office changes with a change of Government. That is not so to the same extent with regard to other Government departments.

Item agreed to.
High Commissioner's Office-salaries, $26,640 ; Contingencies, $76,586.
