speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is exactly the same vote as last year except for the statutory increases.
Supply-High Commissioner

We have noticed through the press that a gentleman from the city of Toronto, a great personal friend of the Prime Minister, and a stalwart of the Liberal party, has been appointed to the very important position of High Commissioner for Canada at London. It seems to me that we might well have some statement from the Prime Minister as to any changes which he proposes to have made through that gentleman in the working of that office. I understand that it has been his stated policy that any announcement with regard to matters of policy, and I regard this as a matter of policy, shall be made to Parliament. I believe that principle has been honoured more in the breach than the observance by the present Prime Minister, because I notice that the present High Commissioner was banqueted on a number of occasions, on one of which at least I think the Prime Minister was present. I would suggest that this is an opportune moment for the Prime Minister to state to the House and to the country what changes he proposes shall take place with respect to the working of the office of the High Commissioner at London under the new incumbency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may answer my hon. friend by saying that of recent years there have been representatives of different government departments in London, for instance the Immigration Department, the Pension Board, Trade and Commerce and other departments, each of which has carried on its work by direct communication with the departmental heads here, but there has not been supervision under one head, of all the government agencies in the Old Country. It is proposed that the High Commissioner who has just been appointed shall exercise supervision over all the government agencies in London, to co-ordinate the work as effectively as possible, and to be the one channel through which the departments of the Government will communicate with the Government offices in Great Britain. That is the one change, I think, of importance.
Another change that has been suggested is that in making further appointments to the office of the High Commissioner in London, an effort be made to secure Canadians to fill the vacancies that occur on the staff.

The Prime Minister has just covered the point I was going to raise. I have noticed at different times at that
[Mr Mnrlcpn^io TCinsr. I
office in London that there were a great many on the staff who were not Canadians, and while I have no objection in any shape or form to British born being in that office, I believe that the Canadian office in London or anywhere else is one that should be filled by Canadians. I was going to ask my right hon. friend the Prime Minister to make a statement in regard to that, and I am very pleased to hear that it is the intention of the Government to fill that office as far as possible with Canadians.

I am getting afraid of the overtime working of this word "coordination". I do not know what is meant by co-ordination now. Perhaps we had better defer these estimates. How are you going to co-ordinate the various offices in England, the Immigration Office, the Trade and Commerce Office, and all the others under the High Commissioner? The Trade and Commerce officers are officers of the Trade and Commerce Department and will be subject to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Immigration officers, Mr. Obed Smith and those under him, are under the Minister of the Interior. Similarly any officers that may be over there in the interests of the Railway Department will be under the Minister of Railways. How are they to be under the High Commissioner, and then each in turn under his minister here? That kind of coordination will simply mean chaos. It will simply mean a division of authority, a conflict of interest, friction and trouble, so if that is going to be the fruitage of all the promises made at these banquets I am afraid it would be better to eliminate coordination from the dictionary altogether. Would the Prime Minister tell us to what extent these men are to be responsible to the High Commissioner, and to what extent they are to be responsible to their ministers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I might tell my hon. friend that when Sir George Perley, who was High Commissioner under his government, returned to Canada to tender his resignation, he informed me that he thought it very important that in some manner the High Commissioner should have supervising authority over all branches of the Canadian Government in England. He stated that during recent years different agencies of the Canadian Government in England were becoming accustomed to taking up matters on their own account with the British Government

Supply-Militia
without any knowledge on the part of the High Commisioner as to what was going on, and frequently this had resulted in two or three different departments of the government of Canada dealing with the Home Government without the knowledge of each other and with consequent confusion and a great deal of overlapping. He pointed out that from his view it was most important that, if possible, as had been originally intended, all communication between the Home Government and the different departments of the Canadian Government carrying on work there should be through the High Commissioner's office or with its knowledge. It was, I say quite frankly, on the suggestion and recommendation of Sir George Perley as the result of his experience as to what was best and most necessary in connection with that office, that the present Government was pleased to take the line of policy which it has taken, the advantages of which, I think, are so obvious as to commend it to everyone.

That is a very different thing indeed to placing these officers under the High Commisioner. What Sir George Perley evidently intended was this, that in so far as these officers acting under the instructions of their respective ministers had anything to do with the British Government they should act through the High Commissioner's office, making that the medium between them and the British Government. But that does not place them under the High Commissioner in any way whatsoever. It merely makes the High Commissioner the agency of communication for all the departments. There is no supervision exercisable by him at all, nor is there any co-ordination. There is merely the ultization of the High Com-misioner's office for the purposes of communication with the British Government. That is all I have ever heard Sir George Perley urge, myself, and that does not in any way detract from the authority of the minister over his officers or place any of the supervising power, over an officer of a department in the hands of the High Commissioner in London. That, I should think, would be detrimental to the service, and I venture to suggest that if the High Commissioner asked for it, his request would not be endorsed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the one hand or the Minister of the Interior on the other. To make him a medium of communication is wholly another thing. He is in no sense a supervisor of their work.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question which applies not only to this department, but possibly to some others. As prices are going down, we ought to expect some reduction in the items included under the heading "Contingencies"- clerical assistance, rent, insurance, income tax, fuel, light, stationery, etc. I notice here, and I have noticed in connection with the other estimates we have discussed this evening, that no reduction in these items is indicated. I feel a little uneasy lest with the falling prices we are really enlarging or increasing our expenditures.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is very difficult to tell exactly how much will be required for this service during any given year. It has been found advisable to vote annually a certain sum, all of which may not be required. We are simply following that course: we are voting, in
10 p.m. round figures, the same as was voted last year. If the full amount is not needed, the balance will be returned to the Treasurey, but if an insufficient amount were voted, embarrassment might result. With the business growing as it is, what is saved through reduced costs may be taken up in increased and extended duties.

Well I do not feel quite satisfied with the answer, although it may be a sufficient one as applying to this particular item. If we vote more than will be required, we may be giving encouragement to extravagance, and surely that is something we ought to avoid. It might be that embarrassment would be caused if less than the amount required were voted. But if that applies to this particular department, it surely does not apply so much to the departments nearer home.
What is the salary of the High Commissioner?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am informed it is $10,000.

Item agreed to.
Civil government-Militia and Defence- salaries and contingencies, $615,577.
['I am informed it is $10,000.']

I have a very sincere sympathy with the minister who is in charge of this very onerous department of government, and I commend his efforts to economize. I find that he has reduced the staff by nine, making a net saving of $925, which is very commendable indeed. I understand that the minister is going to "co-
Supply-Militia

ordinate" several of the government services: militia, naval, police, and air services are to be merged. I think the items which have just been called ought to carry, but I sincerely trust that when the minister gets through with his efforts in the co-ordination of these four departments, there will be something left beyond air.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Militia and Defence) : I may say that I tried to use the word "synchronize" instead of the word "co-ordinate," but it did not seem to fit in.
The "syn" part is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Well, some of us do inherit things. The estimates for civil government are practically what they were last year. We have reduced the number of employes by nine, but we are providing for $24,000 by way of annual increase according to the classification. If you will permit me, Mr. Chairman, I will read a statement which the officers of the department have given me; it will cover the case fairly and generally:
The original permanent civil establishment of the Department of Militia and Defence for the fiscal year 1921-22 (i.e., the year of readjustment after the war and after reclassification) numbered 441. The Estimates for that year were prepared in the fall of 1920 and were not submitted to Parliament till four or five months later. Owing to the rapid falling off of the work during that time, it was difficult to make any close or accurate forecast of the needs of the department for twelve to fifteen months in advance. Accordingly, when the Estimates were presented to Parliament it was thought that 42 of the 441 positions would not be required and, on the suggestion of the Minister of Militia, the money for these positions was not voted, leaving a net establishment of 399 persons.
Later in the year it was found that two of these positions would be required, and as the incumbents had been in the service for many years and there was a surplus in the appropriation, their salaries were paid, bringing the establishment to 401 persons.
During the year, a committee on reorganization, consisting of a representative of the Civil Service Commission, the Assistant Deputy Minister, and another general representative of the Department, together with the Chief of the branch being reorganized, found during their investigations that it was expedient to create fourteen new permanent civil positions in the various branches of the department, thus making the establishment 415, but, at the same time, this Committee recommended that 24 of the then existing positions should he abolished, reducing the establishment to 391. The recommendation to Privy Council for the new establishment embracing these changes has been put forward by the Civil Service Commission and is now before Privy Council.
One account clerk, a returned soldier, still suffering from wounds, is carried super-
[Mr. Mewburn.j
numerary to establishment but for which no vote is required, reducing the actual establishment for which Estimates are being put forward to 390 as compared with 399 for last year.
Attached hereto is a balance sheet showing the changes in the establishment since April 1st, 1921, and the money value of these changes.
It should be noted in connection with the total amount voted for the fiscal year 1921-22, $586,431, and the total amount required for 1922-23, $585,577, that although the saving of $854 seems small, the amount for the coming year includes provision for the annual increases in salaries of $60, $120 or $180 to 390 employes and had there not been savings as described above and in reclassification, the requirements for this year must have exceeded the vote for last year by the estimated amount of those increases, viz: about $24,000.
Tell us when the work of re-classification was undertaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It was begun in 1920 and
completed about three months ago.
I see; we have at least enabled the Minister to effect such reductions as he has made.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He had quite a willingness to do it before.
I notice that about 20 junior clerks have been released but that in place of them pretty nearly the same number of senior clerks have been appointed. How is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In 1921-22 there were 27 junior clerks and in 1922-23 there were 16. Then of junior file clerks there were 33 in 1921-22, and 16 in 1922-23.

Further up the list there are three more junior file clerks, making twenty altogether that have gone, and on the other side of the page nearly the same number of seniors have been added. That is to say, on the one side about twenty juniors are represented to have gone, and on the other side some twenty seniors have been added.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If we are to take all the good that is to come out of the Civil Service Commission we must accept the things to which we object as well. These changes are due to the re-classification made with ' the full consent and approval and with the assistance of the Civil Service Commission. Under that re-classification these changes were made. On the whole, my hon. friend will see that there is a reduction in the number of employees.

With the decrease of activity in my hon. friend's department, so widely advertised and so marked with the

Supply-Militia
reduction of staffs throughout the country, why is it necessary to have three .purchasing agents instead of one? I should think with the reduction of activities throughout the country, one junior purchasing agent would have been able to carry on without adding two more to the staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the exact number the department had before the war. Under the re-classification the staff has been reduced' to a pre-war condition.
But the number has increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no increase
anywhere except through re-classification.
Then this is a case where figures lie.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I wil not give the reverse statement. I might say this, Mr. Chairman, in reply to the remark of my hon. friend as to decreased activities: During the war period a great many hundred temporary employees had of necessity to be taken into the department. The estimates of this department ought now to be credited with a further reduction of $600,000; instead of the reduction being $1,100,000 it actually is $1,700,000. These temporary employees were engaged after the war and they were paid out of Demobilization Vote, consequently their namies, or jthe amounts paid to them, do not appear in the Civil Service list. But the reduction that takes place in the Department on March 31st, of 400 employees-which reduction I dislike personally very much to make-means a saving of $600,000 more than appears in these estimates. In other words, had not that reduction been made the vote under War Claims, which appears in another place, would have been $600,000 larger than it is.
I notice it is now a good deal larger than last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The War Appropriation?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Well, I tell my right hon. friend, since he insists, that if he had not taken $3,000,000 out of the Demobilization Fund to give it to the Dominion Steel Company we would have paid a lot of these debts this year.
And I tell the minister that with that taken out, an obligation which undoubtedly rose from the war, there was still a large balance over, and the

whole amount asked for last year was for a sum much less than the sum asked for this year, although we are a year further from the war. I would like to ask the minister how much of this reduction was effected or provided for in the year 1921 in sums that are attributable to and paid out of demobilization or, as it is called now, "Adjustment of War Claims"?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These included in the $600,000 have been made since the present Government came into office and are to take effect from April 1st, the beginning of the next fiscal year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

I do not think this item should carry, although we have had some usesful discussion on it. In the absence of the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who was Minister of Militia in the late Government, and who will be back, I think, to-morrow-at all events by Wednesday-I think the item should stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not going to press for its adoption but we will have all the other Militia estimates open for discussion, and I would like to say that I would have had my bill for uniting the different defence departments under one head up to-day had it not been at the request of the ex-Minister of Militia who asked me to defer it until he came back. He raised no objection to going on with the estimates.

I think it is correct that the hon. member for Wellington made that request-I know he mentioned to me that he would ask that the bill should stand over-but his request would have had just as much application to these estimates. I do not suppose he anticipated the estimates would be gone on with, there are other estimates that can be taken up.
Before we pass from this item may I ask the minister if this sum we are voting here will cover the administration of the co-ordinated departments after the co-ordination takes place?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. It is a difficult situation to form an opinion as to the various departments as the amalgamation is not completed and each department is asking for its own estimates; but in the other departments we expect to have a saving

in some of them at least-much more than will appear on the surface. Under the heading of Civil Government, part of the estimates we are asking prac-
Supply-Militia

tically total the same amount as before till we have an opportunity, after the bill for the amalgamation goes through, to find out just where we can make a saving. It is confidently expected, for instance, that the executive work of the Air Force and the Militia can be merged; I am afraid it will become necessary to make a large reduction in the number of temporary employees on the staff of the Air Board-in fact I know it will have to be done, much to my regret. Then we have the Naval Service which we hope to amalgamate as far as possible-the purchasing department and the departmental services as we might call them. In the mounted police, which has always conducted its departmental services separately, we hope to make quite a large saving; but what these savings will be I cannot tell from the estimates for Civil Government until I have had an opportunity to bring the different departmental staffs together. I shall then be able to tell what the actual saving will he in that respect. As I say, each department, at the present time, is asking for its Civil Government estimates practically the same amount as before. When I get the amalgamation into one department effected, I hope to be able to make quite a saving in Civil Government, as well as in the other branches. It must be remembered that a great deal of what we call temporary services, although they are not perhaps paid for out of that vote, always have been carried on by temporary and not by permanent employees,
If we can point out to the minister when he brings his bill down where a million or two can be saved in this department, he might not need all the money asked for in this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am afraid it would not interfere with the civil staff very much, if any. It is like a business. You have your organization and a great deal of the work is carried on by temporary employees. So far as the permanent employees are concerned, unless we drop the organization altogether, I am afraid we need not expect much reduction in the civil staff.
Item stands.
Naval Service, salaries, $215,220.
This is an increase over last year of some $5,130.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The increases are all statutory.
One would think, with all the co-ordination going on, that there might he a diminution.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The only reply I can make to that is that the Civil Service Commission is responsible for every increase there.
They are the customary statutory increases?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Is the whole staff to be continued? The minister had not the privilege of being here last session and the previous session, or he would understand my amazement now in finding the civil list added to even in this awful department of Naval Service.

Suppose the work of
the department were wiped out altogether, would the minister say that, because the Civil Service Commission had made appointments to the staff and the staff had been organized, it would therefore continue in perpetuity? If the work is cut down, does not the staff come down, even in spite of the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will explain that we do not expect to have a saving until we get our reorganization effected. That is one of the difficulties of reorganization. We are not just in a position to say how great the saving will be. These estimates do not all belong to the naval service proper. These include very many other services besides what is sometimes called the Naval Service. They include fishery protection, which is undertaken by the British navy to some extent. They include the wireless telegraphy, the hydrographic staff, the tidal surveys and so on. Several items are put under the naval expenditures which are not justly chargeable to the naval service at all, and I might point out that notwithstanding the criticism that, while last year the naval service estimates for the naval service alone, without the other services were $2,500,000, this year I have reduced them with one stroke of the pen to $1,500,000.

My hon. friend did not answer the question I asked. I wanted to know, as a general question, not dealing with his department more than any other, though it does deal with his department; when the work of a department is cut down, is it prohibited by the Civil Service Commission, as implied by his own remarks, that the organization should be cut down at

Supply-Naval
the same time? Is the cutting down absolutely prevented by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I would not think so.

His remark suggested
the question. If the minister says it is not prevented, and he has cut down the estimate a million and a half-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A little over a million.

That must mean the cutting down of the work of the department to a great extent. It would seem to me, that under those circumstances, that would permit of the cutting down also of the headquarters staff.
' Mr. HANSON: Will there be two deputy ministers of this department, of defence? There is the Deputy Minister of Naval Service, the Deputy Minister of Militia and the Deputy Minister of Fisheries. Is the hon. minister going to have three or four of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will explain that situation more fully when I get my bill for the amalgamation of the different services.

Does the minister think we ought to consider that item before he knows what he wants? He apparently does not know what he wants, and apparently cannot give any explanation as to what he wants. Why should we consider this matter till the bill is brought down? Referring to another matter, he says all the changes are the result of the action of the Civil Service Commission. I never knew the Civil Service Commission created vacancies or positions, nor do I think they are doing it now. We are going to have the work of the department cut down to a very large extent, but I see we have one inspector where there was none before. We have one accountant in grade 4 where there was none before, and six head clerks at headquarters where there were formerly four. We have an accountant in grade 2 where there was none before. Then, we have two new secretaries to the executive, whatever that is; I suppose that is to keep track of the contractions that are going to be made in the service. We have two secretaries to the executive to work out the reductions that the hon. gentleman is going to make; we have six senior account clerks as against five before; we have six senior clerks as against five; we have sixteen clerk stenographers as against eleven; five clerk typists as against one, and seven file clerks as against
27J
six, and we are told this is all due to the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Get down to the totals.

I am taking the explanation of the minister. The explanation given by my hon. friend was that all these changes were made by the Civil Service Commission, and I am pointing out at a glance that he has not been quite properly instructed.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Notwithstanding my hon. friend's wonderful information, he dodged successfully or unsuccessfully the Civil Service Commission while he was in office. We have the same number of clerks as before, and owing to re-classification, their status has been changed. If he looks at the totals he will understand it.

I would like to call attention to the same thing that I had occasion to refer to a few minutes ago. There are at the foot of this list some fifteen or. sixteen junior clerks who have lost their positions, and those positions have been taken by senior clerks at much higher salaries. Is that also under the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is absolutely under the commission.
It is time the department of the minister took something into its own hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman vote for that?
Yes, I will vote for the abolition of the commission.

Is my hon.
friend serious in stating that the Civil Service Commission dismissed a large number of the more poorly paid clerks in the department? That was the question that was put.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I did not say anything of the kind.
That is the question that I understood was put by my hon. friend, and the answer was that they were dismissed by the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That was not the
question nor the answer. My hon. friend is wrong both ways.

My question was quite plain. I inquired why it was that fifteen junior clerks had lost their jobs and senior clerks at higher salaries had taken their places.
Supply-Naval

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend is, I think, mistaken. He should not be led astray by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) who knows nothing about the Civil Service Commission. Of course, he had some branches under him, but they were not under the Civil Service Commission.
I am asking a plain question.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is a reclassification of junior clerks into higher positions. The hon. member will probably find most of these junior clerks who, he thinks, were dismissed, occupying better positions owing to reclassification.

That is one reason why I am in favour of abolishing the commission. Let me just look into the explanation of the minister. There are five junior typists at a salary of $720. Does the minister mean to say that those men are now in amongst senior clerks at a salary of $1,140? That is a pretty big increase for one year. I do not think the minister has made a proper explanation, because these junior clerks are at such a low salary and the senior clerks at such a relatively high salary. As I understand the matter, the usual increase is only $120 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Most of these stenographers are ladies and not men. I say again to my hon. friend that as long as we have the Civil Service Commission, the departments are bound to carry out the classifications under the commission in this respect.

Is there anything in the Civil Service Act that would prevent the minister from reducing this staff? Another objection which I have to this proposition is this:	The minister tells us
that there has been a reduction in expenditure in the outside service of some million dollars. In other words, men in the outside service are losing their jobs, and yet the overhead of the department remains stationary. In ordinary business, when your business goes away from you, you must bring down your overhead to correspond.

What is the extent of our Naval Service in Canada? This, I understand, covers the fleet which, if newspaper reports are true, is somewhere out in the Atlantic at the present time; but beyond one cruiser, two destroyers and two submarines, that, I think, constitute the fleet,

what is the Naval Service of Canada? I was going to add-and, perhaps, the minister could give the explanation when he rises to answer my question-that it seems to me that 125 of a staff in the head office of the Naval Service is quite a considerable staff to run our limited Naval Service.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As I pointed out a moment ago, that would be what the country understands as the Naval Service, but the Naval Service includes probably half a dozen other branches. It includes the Fishery Protection Service, in which we have six fishery protection vessels. It also includes the Hydrographic Survey in which we have five vessels. Then, under the arrangement with the British Admiralty, when we passed the Naval Service Act in 1910, we have to provide for the care of the docks at Esquimalt and Halifax. We have at the present time a school at Halifax and a school at Esquimalt in addition to the ships to which my hon. friend refers. These ships were presented by the British Admiralty to the Dominion of Canada through the late government, and they were accepted by the late government.
A great mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be prepared to discuss that, but not on the civil estimates. That is the situation, and these two destroyers, two submarines and one cruiser are now the property of Canada on account of the presentation made of them through the late government to Canada.

It appears to me that the same objection might be made to passing this estimate as was raised to the militia and defence estimates. If it is intended to co-ordinate the three branches of the service, it seems a strange procedure to continue the appointments under the head of civil government, to pass the three civil government estimates, and then later on to have an explanation by the minister as to how these savings are going to be made. It would be more satisfactory to know what the Government proposes to do in the matter before we pass all the estimates for civil government. It may be that many of these officials will not be required. If the Government cannot do anything themselves in making an adjustment on account of the Civil Service Commission, there is something radically wrong. I quite appreciate that, where three branches of the Government are to be co-ordinated and brought under one head, a min-

Supply-Naval
ister would naturally desire to have some reforms made. If it is owing to the fact that the Civil Service Commission exercises so much control over him that his hands are tied, something should be done about the matter. Surely if those three branches are brought under the one department, some very radical changes can be made and great savings effected. It has been intimated that there is going to be a very large saving made in the Air Force, the Naval Service and the Militia. If that be the case, surely as the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) has pointed out, there must be some reductions made in the overhead charges in connection with this, as there would be in any business that was carried on on a business basis. It seems a most unusual thing to pass all these items under the head of civil government, and then to discuss how these reforms shall be put into effect. This item could surely stand along with the other two to which the same complaint might be raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend is, perhaps, not quite clear on this point. These services must be continued, because any changes that are made cannot be completed for perhaps three months. The bill may not pass. Indeed, my bill would have been before the House instead of these estimates, if it had not been for the Opposition. This is not my fault. It is necessary to pass these estimates in order to carry on the work as we have it, until we can complete the reorganization, and I am inclined to believe that the shortest period in which we can get the reorganization effected is three months. It is not an easy matter to get together four different departments, and to undertake to say what the adjustment is going to be until we get them together. We may find that one man will answer where we have two now. I do not know which man, I do not know what salary, and until we can get the amalgamation effected, which will take some months, we must have estimates passed to carry on with our staff.

In the Department of Naval Service there is a deputy minister at $6,000, and an assistant deputy at $4,200; under Militia and Defence a deputy minister at $6,000, and an assistant deputy at $5,100. In the Air Board the total is given as $75,000. I presume the Chairman of the Air Board has the same status as a deputy minister ?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The minister is chairman of the board and he gets nothing in addition for it.
But I thought there was a Chairman of the Air Board too.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a Deputy Chairman, General Gwatkin.
I presume he gets $5,000 or $6,000. His salary would be part of the $75,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: General Gwatkin is a military man, but at my request he is acting as Deputy Chairman of the Air Board at the present time. Colonel Biggar was Deputy Chairman and he got no salary whatever; he acted for nothing. General Gwatkin was Inspector General of the Air Force, and, as I say, is Acting Deputy Chairman of the board. I may add that the Acting Deputy Chairman is retiring after a few months'leave of absence.

As it stands, I presume he receives $5,000, or possibly $6,000. Turning to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Controller, I take it, would receive $5,000 or $6,000. We have, all told, seven or eight highly paid officials, and if there is to be a co-ordination it is to be presumed some of the officers must be dispensed with. Surely it is important to know if that is to take place before we are asked to vote these salaries. If you are to have only one deputy and one assistant deputy under the co-ordination, then a lot of salaries will not be needed, and we ought to have some knowledge on that point before being asked to vote these items. The same line of reasoning no doubt applies to clerks and other officials in the various branches of the service, but for convenience sake I single out the most highly paid officials in order to ascertain the minister's views. I appreciate what he says, that it will take a little time to effect the reorganization, but perhaps it would be well to let the Estimates stand until the bill is before the House. If the bill does not pass I can understand that all these officers will have to be kept on. If, on the other hand, the bill passes and there is a co-ordination, most of these salaries would not be required for more than three months at the outside.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is a difficulty in dropping these Estimates until we know how we are to make the reorganization. The hon. member possibly thinks that it is an easy matter to get the different staffs to work in, but until I have the full author-
Supply-Naval

ity of Parliament to commence the work of reorganization I do not know just what may be done. It will take months to work it out exactly in detail, and in the meantime we have assured the House of our intention to cut down expenses, by cutting down more than $1,000,000 in the Naval Estimates. That is good evidence that we intend to make reductions. Of the civil government expenditures, only 46 per cent refers to Naval Service at all; 54 per cent is for other services. When hon. gentlemen talk about cutting down on civil government, they are talking about something which they cannot grasp; nor can I grasp it fully until I have had a chance to take off my coat and go into it and decide what I am to do. Not a dollar of this money that is not absolutely necessary will be expended, but in the meantime the staffs have to carry on until we can effect the amalgamation.

A 25 per cent vote would take care of the situation for at least three months. I think the Estimates should stand and the minister could go on with the bill. Upon the result of the bill we could deal more intelligently with the items.

I endorse what has been said by the hon. member. We are absolutely in the dark to-night. Let us have the bill, and we can intelligently discuss the Estimates. Discussing Estimates for three or four departments that are to be co-ordinated, seems to me rather ridiculous. Why cannot we wait until the exMinister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) returns, have the bill presented by the present minister (Mr. Graham), and then approach the Estimates in an intelligent and satisfactory way? We all desire to carry on the affairs of the country, but we are rather in the dark at the present time, and if the minister is at sea we are out in the ocean.
Does the reduction of $1,000,000 which the minister refers to apply to the Naval Service proper or to other branches connected with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It applies to Naval Service proper and to other services too.

The minister says that 46 per cent of the activities represented here are concerned yith the N aval Service. What becomes of the other 54 per cent? I think my hon. friend has made a serious charge in connection with the Civil Service Commission. I do not profess to have looked into the matter as he has done, but for the purpose of appre-
TMr. Graham.]
ciating the facts, I would ask him to give me the names of the junior clerks who were reclassified and promoted, showing from what ratings they were promoted and what ratings they were given, and when that was done.

While the minister is looking up the information, I should like to emphasize a fact stated by previous speakers. I was one of the first to mention that I did not see any reason why the Civil Service Commission should be permitted to keep the overhead as high as it was, when the rest of the staff had been cut down. In looking over the details I find that it is as high as it ever was. Take the Department of Militia. There are 390 employees provided for this year as against 399, a decrease of 9; but in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police there is an increase of 8-22 as against 14; while in the Department of Naval Service the number is absolutely the same as it was before. So that with one exception, there are the same number of employees in the three departments as there were under the expensive operation which the late government carried on, according to my hon. friend. Certainly, with the cutting down that he is doing-and I have no reason to doubt that he is cutting down-I think there will be plenty of opportunity for him to reduce the staff. Seeing that he is reducing the outside staff he might effect economies in the inside service, and I agree that this vote should be held until we can get more details. At the moment the minister is not in a position to tell us what he is going to do. To keep him in good humour I might remind him that last year I well remember sitting behind the minister when his Estimates were up, and when hon. gentlemen opposite who were then on this side of the House took up very much more time discussing Estimates than we have done, sometimes even prolonging the discussion for a week or two; so we have a long distance to go before hon. gentlemen opposite are equalled in their blocking tactics of last year and the year before.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In reply to my hon.
friend's question as to General Gwatkin's salary, he receives a pension from the British Government, and I am informed that the amount he receives from us is $3,500. I might say, so far as giving details is concerned, that it is impossible for me to give them now. The best I could do would be to make a blind guess. It will take three

Supply-Naval
42.'}
months to make the amalgamation, and if Parliament takes the ground that it must know all the details before we proceed with the work, I say that that is a very unbusinesslike stand to take, and that nobody would take it in their own private business. We cannot proceed to amalgamate these branches until given authority to carry on.	*

But under the amalgamation we should not need the same amount of money. My hon. friend admits that he will probably cut the staffs down, but here we find an increase in the Estimates of three different branches. We should not be required to vote an equal or greater amount than was voted last year.

It seems to me that the
minister is asking us to construct a large frame work into which can be fitted the various organizations that have existed in the past. If the bill he proposes for the co-ordination of the various branches should pass the House, the structure we are now building by the passing of these Estimates will have to be wrecked to a certain extent. It does seem to me that the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) expressed the proper view, and that the minister should bring his bill before the House and give us at least some idea of what he proposes in the way of co-ordinating these various branches. Then the members of the committee would be in a better position to make suggestions to the minister as to how the moneys required for the administration of this amalgamated department could be provided. I hope the minister will see his way to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Cumberland.

Before the committee
rises I would like to say a word in regard to an impression which I think the committee has gained from the minister. I do not think he intended to give a wrong impression, but I think the committee got the impression that the Civil Service Commission is responsible for what they are not responsible for at all. Notwithstanding the Civil Service Commission and the Civil Service Act, as the minister well knows-I do not think he tried to mislead the committee or had any thought of doing so-the Government can make any reduction that it sees fit. The Government may accept the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission as to what organization is necessary for a certain work, but the responsibility of accepting it is on the Government. The Government can dismiss as many officers as they desire. If there were anything in the act restraining or abbreviating the right of the Government or the authority or responsibility of the Government in respect of the public service, I would feel, like the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin), that the time had come for an amendment, but that is not in the power of the commission at all. That is not its responsibility; that is the responsibility wholly of the Government. I commend the attitude of the minister in allowing this item to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have no objection to
letting it stand. I was just saying that I cannot tell what is going to happen until I have the authority to have it happen. Let me point out to my right hon. friend that I did not make any suggestion that the Civil Service Commission dismissed people. He was listening to his desk-mate, not to me. I fully explained that probably none of the junior clerks referred to were dismissed, but simply became seniors in the re-classification. The ex-Minister of Finance put his own interpretation upon that. He was the one to talk about the commission dismissing them.
I think that the committee got the impression, not that the commission dismissed anybody, but that they prevented the minister from dismissing them.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I never suggested that. It was the ex-Minister of Finance.

I would urge upon the Government the necessity of giving consideration to the demand which exists throughout the country for a reduction in the staffs of the Civil Service. The impression prevails generally throughout the country, and is shared in by myself to a very large extent, that civil servants are treading on one another's toes, so tremendously is the Service over-manned. To what extent that is true we are not in a position to say, but since coming here we have not seen anything that would tend to dispel the impression that we had when we came. If the Government could do anything to dispel the impression that the service is tremendously over-manned or over-womaned, as the case may be, or could do anything to reduce the overhead expenditure, I am sure it would receive the commendation of the people of this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Before moving that the committee rise and report progress, I might perhaps explain the position in which the Government is placed in regard to this vote. To-day is the 27th of March, and in four days we shall have entered upon a new fiscal year. Unless the Government is to dismiss immediately all employees whose services it will not be necessary to retain; once this amalgamation takes effect, these amounts will have to be voted to cover the interval at least, and all the Government is asking at the present time is to allow the vote for civil government to go through so that the clerks at present employed in these different positions may be retained until the minister has had time to effect the reorganization proposed under the new bill. Before that bill becomes law it will have to receive its three readings in this House, and then pass the Senate; and until that has been done it will not be possible for the minister to begin the work of consolidation. That is our only reason for seeking to get through these votes as they stand.
My remarks applied not merely to the Militia Department but to all departments of the service.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Government is in hearty agreement with my hon. friend in its desire to prevent any overlapping.
Progress reported.
